rv.q: Kinney and his superb cast are attuned to the silent undercurrents of Greenberg’s writing as much as the sly flourishes of wit and cruelty and the elegant streams of prose-like dialogue, making The Babylon Line an idiosyncratic pleasure.
“The Babylon Line” is one of those modest little gems that contains sparks of white light if you look hard enough.
Richard Greenberg’s rich, intentionally untidy new play, “The Babylon Line,” begins with the words “the end.”
The play itself, for all its enviable eloquence, has problems.
Instead, it’s where I lost interest in The Babylon Line, and I felt that Greenberg did as well, since the ending — the several endings — are a muddle of inconclusiveness.
“The Babylon Line” remains stranded in the search for one.

The Babylon Line is a play, not a novel or a semiotics paper, the gesture deflates as quickly as a pricked balloon, and comes to seem less like a clever feint than a premature epitaph for a story that fails to thrive.
Greenberg builds a marvelously complete universe with his characters; it's a world that, as 1967 unfolds, will be forever changed.
Greenberg sacrifices the tragedy of the moment for the comedy of the long perspective — and we are grateful to him for it.
Fortunately, his many detours and transgressions work only to keep us riveted for this two-and-a-half hour comedy.
The quiet, funny script resonates with the evergreen themes of community, desire, and self-discovery.
THE BABYLON LINE is still a pleasing excursion with good humor and warm pathos.
Happily, it doesn't much matter, because Greenberg's eloquence and sly wit translate into scenes of biting beauty when the students start reading their writing.
Even so, The Babylon Line could stand to get where it's going faster and better.

Although The Babylon Line is as funny and literate as his previous works, Greenberg seems to be struggling to unite all the separate threads into a smooth whole, awkwardly depending on the central character’s breaking the fourth wall.

But, for all its cleverness, The Babylon Line (named after a section of the Long Island Rail Road) suffers from a basic dramatic flaw: both Aaron and Joan’s characters remain frustratingly static throughout its two hours.
The Babylon Line bulges in odd places, seems to stall in others, and tends to feel alternately as if nothing were happening and too much had been crammed in.
The Babylon Line, while highly listenable, never finds the right balance between its contrived storyline, self-conscious dialogue, and colorful but artificial characters.
But what emerges is a muddle of ideas and styles.
If that’s all you ask of this play—to turn out “reasonably well”—you’ll be more than pleased that you bought your ticket.
Like the Long Island Rail Road train line that this play refers to, Richard Greenberg’s The Babylon Line works quite well about half the time, and the rest seems to get delayed or derailed.
But never do you feel close to the people you have met.
Unfortunately, while the cast deftly paints portraits of familiarity, the play fails to draw sparks.
By the end of the play it felt like we had just sat for over two hours in Mr. Greenberg’s therapy session where even he couldn't figure it out.

It’s a funny, smart, gently revelatory play that digs beyond the commonplace insight that great depths can lurk behind the conformity of suburbia — though it does make that point — to also consider the unimaginable, unpredictable paths our lives can take.
Tough, tender, interesting, a bit of Long Island history, and a generally magical evening in the theatre.
THE BABYLON LINE is an enjoyable, though flawed, play superbly acted.
